text: Given a non-negative integer x, return the square root of x rounded down to the nearest integer. You may not use any built-in exponent function — no pow of x, zero point five.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — rounded down means for x equals eight I return two, since two squared is four and three squared is nine. So really I'm looking for the largest m with m times m at most x. Are there any constraints on the input size?
x goes from zero up to two to the thirty-first, minus one.

That's the whole ballgame, so let me say it now. The answer itself is small — at most forty-six thousand three hundred forty. But the numbers I square along the way are not going to be small, and I'll come back to that when I pick my types. Let me run through the example. Take x equals eight, and ask for each candidate: is m squared bigger than eight? Zero, one and two say false; three, four and five say true. False, false, false, then true forever — it flips once and never flips back. The answer, two, is the last false, sitting right before the first true. Also: is zero a valid input? I want to be sure my method handles it without a special case.
Yes, zero is valid. It should return zero.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to count up from zero until the square passes x. That's square root of x time, about forty-six thousand steps at worst. It would pass, but it ignores the structure I just noticed. This problem reminds me of binary search on a predicate. That row of falses and trues is exactly what binary search wants. I never need a sorted array — I need one yes-or-no question whose answer flips at most once as I walk along. Here the question is m squared greater than x, and it's monotone because squaring is increasing on non-negative numbers. So: binary search for the first true, then step back one to get the last false. That's log x — about thirty-one rounds instead of forty-six thousand. And it never touches a double, so there's no rounding to argue about.

Here's the plan. One: ask whether m squared is greater than x. Two: search from zero to x plus one — true moves right to mid, false moves left past mid. Three: return left minus one. Neither offset can be dropped. The plus one guarantees a true exists, since x plus one, squared, always beats x; with just x, zero would return negative one. The minus one turns the first true into the last false. One thing worth flagging — mid squared peaks on the very first round, not at the answer: about two to the sixtieth, roughly half a billion times INT MAX. So left, right and mid all have to be long long. It's tempting to say the answer is only forty-six thousand, so int is fine — that's backwards. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop: if mid squared is greater than x, right moves to mid; otherwise left moves past mid; then I return left minus one. One thing worth flagging: the cast in long long of x, plus one. Without it, x plus one is computed in int before being widened, and at INT MAX that's signed overflow. And I want to be honest about how I know that matters, because it surprised me. Built at O two, the version without the cast still returned forty-six thousand three hundred forty for INT MAX — the right answer. Then the undefined behaviour sanitizer immediately reported signed integer overflow on INT MAX plus one. The optimizer just happened to emit code that worked. Passing tests proves the logic, not the types.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. x is eight, so left is zero and right is nine. The highlighted row is where it locks in: in round three, mid is three and nine is greater than eight, so right drops to three. Now left and right both sit on three — exactly the first true from my earlier table. Step back one and I get two. Two squared is four, at most eight, while three squared is nine, which isn't. Correct. Let's also test with corner cases. Zero: one round, left becomes one, and it returns zero with no special case. One: one round, returns one. Forty-six thousand three hundred forty squared returns exactly that root, and one below it returns one less. INT MAX returns forty-six thousand three hundred forty in thirty-one rounds.

The time complexity is log x — the range starts at two to the thirty-first and halves each round, so about thirty-one rounds; x equals INT MAX takes exactly thirty-one. The space complexity is constant, three variables. That's thirty-one multiplications versus roughly forty-six thousand for counting up. On the peak magnitude: mid squared tops out at two to the sixtieth, which is twelve and a half percent of LLONG MAX. So long long is enough, but only by a factor of eight — worth knowing rather than assuming. Oh, one more thing — if you widened x itself to long long, this code would break: mid squared would need about a hundred twenty-four bits, and there's no wider built-in type. The fix is to rewrite the comparison as a division: mid greater than x over mid. Same meaning for mid at least one, and it can't overflow.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You wrote out the false-true table in the Understand phase, before choosing anything. That made binary search on a predicate the obvious move instead of a trick you pulled out. You worked out that the largest intermediate value appears on the first round, not near the answer — and called out the tempting wrong reasoning explicitly. And on the missing cast, your tests passed and you still didn't trust them until the sanitizer confirmed it. Most people would have shipped that.
